title: CTS Psalms — Unit 5: Psalm 119, The Word of God

blocks.en: 📖 The Book of Psalms — Unit 5: Psalm 119, The Word of God
blocks.es_reference: 📖 El Libro de los Salmos — Unidad 5: Salmo 119, La Palabra de Dios

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." — Psalm 119:105 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Lámpara es a mis pies tu palabra, y lumbrera a mi camino." — Salmo 119:105 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. The Psalm of the Word
blocks.es_reference: 1. El Salmo de la Palabra

blocks.en: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible — one hundred and seventy-six verses, arranged as an acrostic poem in twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. And almost every single verse mentions the Word of God under one of its many names: the law, the testimonies, the precepts, the statutes, the commandments, the judgments, the word. There are two great psalms of the Word, Psalm 19 and Psalm 119, and this one is the great anthem of a believer who has fallen in love with the Scriptures. We live in a confusing world, and sometimes we do not know which way to turn. The good news of Psalm 119 is that God has answers, and they are often found in His Word.
blocks.es_reference: El Salmo 119 es el capítulo más largo de la Biblia — ciento setenta y seis versículos, dispuestos como un poema acróstico en veintidós secciones, una por cada letra del alfabeto hebreo. Y casi cada versículo menciona la Palabra de Dios bajo uno de sus muchos nombres: la ley, los testimonios, los preceptos, los estatutos, los mandamientos, los juicios, la palabra. Hay dos grandes salmos de la Palabra, el Salmo 19 y el Salmo 119, y este es el gran himno de un creyente que se ha enamorado de las Escrituras. Vivimos en un mundo confuso, y a veces no sabemos hacia dónde volvernos. La buena noticia del Salmo 119 es que Dios tiene respuestas, y a menudo se hallan en Su Palabra.

blocks.en: When we speak of the "Word of God," we should remember that the phrase carries more than one meaning. There is the prophetic Word of God — the message God spoke through His prophets. There is the living Word of God — the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, who is called the Word made flesh. And there is the written Word of God — the Bible, the book we hold in our hands. All three are God speaking, and Psalm 119 teaches us to treasure that speaking with our whole heart.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando hablamos de la "Palabra de Dios," debemos recordar que la frase tiene más de un significado. Está la Palabra profética de Dios — el mensaje que Dios habló por medio de Sus profetas. Está la Palabra viva de Dios — el Señor Jesucristo mismo, que es llamado el Verbo hecho carne. Y está la Palabra escrita de Dios — la Biblia, el libro que tenemos en las manos. Las tres son Dios hablando, y el Salmo 119 nos enseña a atesorar ese hablar con todo el corazón.

blocks.en: 2. Where Wisdom Is Found
blocks.es_reference: 2. Dónde se Halla la Sabiduría

blocks.en: King Solomon, when God offered him anything he wished, asked for wisdom — wisdom that came from God. That is still the great need. And there are three places where God's wisdom comes to us. The first is through prayer. James 1:5 says, "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him." Many times when we pray, God grants a quiet sense of rightness about the way forward.
blocks.es_reference: El rey Salomón, cuando Dios le ofreció cualquier cosa que deseara, pidió sabiduría — sabiduría que venía de Dios. Esa sigue siendo la gran necesidad. Y hay tres lugares donde la sabiduría de Dios nos llega. El primero es por medio de la oración. Santiago 1:5 dice: "Y si alguno de vosotros tiene falta de sabiduría, pídala a Dios, el cual da a todos abundantemente y sin reproche, y le será dada." Muchas veces cuando oramos, Dios concede un sereno sentido de rectitud sobre el camino a seguir.

blocks.en: The second place wisdom comes is through godly counsel. We see this when Moses' father-in-law, Jethro, watched Moses judging the people who came to him all day long — alone — until he was overwhelmed by the needs of others. Jethro gave him wise counsel: appoint God-honoring men as judges to help carry the load (Exodus 18:13-27). That counsel let Moses use the gifts of others for the service of many, rather than trying to manage everything himself. Many times in life we seek wisdom from godly men and women, and almost immediately we know when it is coming from the Lord — because it sounds like Jesus. The third and most critical place, as we will see, is the written Word itself.
blocks.es_reference: El segundo lugar de donde viene la sabiduría es el consejo piadoso. Lo vemos cuando Jetro, el suegro de Moisés, observó a Moisés juzgando todo el día — solo — a la gente que venía a él, hasta quedar abrumado por las necesidades de otros. Jetro le dio un consejo sabio: nombrar hombres temerosos de Dios como jueces para ayudar a llevar la carga (Éxodo 18:13-27). Aquel consejo permitió a Moisés usar los dones de otros para el servicio de muchos, en lugar de tratar de manejarlo todo él mismo. Muchas veces en la vida buscamos sabiduría de hombres y mujeres piadosos, y casi de inmediato sabemos cuándo viene del Señor — porque suena como Jesús. El tercer lugar, y el más crítico, como veremos, es la Palabra escrita misma.

blocks.en: 3. The Lamp and the Light
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Lámpara y la Lumbrera

blocks.en: Psalm 119:105 (NKJV): "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 119:105 (RVG): "Lámpara es a mis pies tu palabra, y lumbrera a mi camino."

blocks.en: But the most critical piece of wisdom comes from the written Word of God, the Bible. It is a lamp to our feet and a light to our path — light enough for the next step, and light enough for the whole journey. The world tries every other path to satisfaction and comes up empty, but the Word of God has guided pilgrims home for thousands of years.
blocks.es_reference: Pero la pieza más crítica de sabiduría viene de la Palabra escrita de Dios, la Biblia. Es lámpara a nuestros pies y lumbrera a nuestro camino — luz suficiente para el próximo paso, y luz suficiente para todo el viaje. El mundo prueba todos los demás caminos hacia la satisfacción y queda vacío, pero la Palabra de Dios ha guiado a los peregrinos a casa por miles de años.

blocks.en: Consider the ward sister in a children's hospital in England who had found life, as she herself said, futile and meaningless. She had waded through book after book and labored through philosophy after philosophy trying to find satisfaction. She had never tried the Bible, because a friend had convinced her with subtle arguments that it could not be true. One day a visitor came to the ward and left a supply of Gospels. She read a copy of John's Gospel, and she believed. "I listened to that voice," she said, "and heard the truth, and found my Savior." The lamp had been within her reach the whole time.
blocks.es_reference: Considere a la enfermera de sala en un hospital de niños en Inglaterra que hallaba la vida, como ella misma decía, fútil y sin sentido. Había recorrido libro tras libro y batallado con filosofía tras filosofía tratando de hallar satisfacción. Nunca había probado la Biblia, porque un amigo la había convencido con argumentos sutiles de que no podía ser verdad. Un día un visitante vino a la sala y dejó unos Evangelios. Ella leyó un ejemplar del Evangelio de Juan, y creyó. "Escuché aquella voz," dijo, "y oí la verdad, y hallé a mi Salvador." La lámpara había estado a su alcance todo el tiempo.

blocks.en: 4. Hidden in the Heart
blocks.es_reference: 4. Guardada en el Corazón

blocks.en: Psalm 119:11 (NKJV): "Your word I have hidden in my heart, that I might not sin against You."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 119:11 (RVG): "En mi corazón he guardado tus dichos, para no pecar contra ti."

blocks.en: Notice where the Word is stored: not merely on a shelf, but in the heart. When the Word is hidden in the heart, it becomes a guard against sin and a treasure that no enemy can confiscate. People may take away your Bible, but they cannot reach into your heart and remove what you have hidden there.
blocks.es_reference: Note dónde se guarda la Palabra: no meramente en un estante, sino en el corazón. Cuando la Palabra está guardada en el corazón, se vuelve una defensa contra el pecado y un tesoro que ningún enemigo puede confiscar. Puede que la gente le quite su Biblia, pero no puede meter la mano en su corazón y quitar lo que usted ha guardado allí.

blocks.en: The Bible That Could Not Be Burned: A boy was ordered by his father to stop reading his Bible, but he slipped it aside and read it anyway despite his father's objections. One day the father caught him, snatched the Bible away, and threw it into the fire. But he noticed the boy was smiling. "Why are you smiling?" he demanded. The boy answered, "I was just thinking that you cannot burn this in here" — and he pointed to his heart. That is the one place the Word is truly safe.
blocks.es_reference: La Biblia que No se Pudo Quemar: A un niño su padre le ordenó dejar de leer su Biblia, pero él la guardaba a un lado y la leía de todos modos a pesar de las objeciones de su padre. Un día el padre lo sorprendió, le arrebató la Biblia y la arrojó al fuego. Pero notó que el niño sonreía. "¿Por qué sonríes?" exigió. El niño respondió: "Solo estaba pensando que esto no lo puede quemar aquí dentro" — y señaló su corazón. Ese es el único lugar donde la Palabra está verdaderamente segura.

blocks.en: 5. The Word That Outlasts Its Enemies
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Palabra que Sobrevive a sus Enemigos

blocks.en: Psalm 119:89 (NKJV): "Forever, O LORD, Your word is settled in heaven."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 119:89 (RVG): "Para siempre, oh Jehová, permanece tu palabra en los cielos."

blocks.en: The Word of God has outlasted every ruler who ever tried to destroy it. Henry V of England once considered Bible reading a crime and passed a law that threatened death or loss of property to anyone caught reading a Bible. But his decrees could not shorten the life of the Scriptures by one minute or lighten their weight by one ounce. The Bible has traveled more roads, been spoken in more languages, and knocked at more doors than any other book ever written. The Scripture is holy; it is altogether different from any other book, because it is the living Word of the living God, and it is settled forever in heaven.
blocks.es_reference: La Palabra de Dios ha sobrevivido a todo gobernante que jamás intentó destruirla. Enrique V de Inglaterra una vez consideró la lectura de la Biblia un crimen y aprobó una ley que amenazaba con la muerte o la pérdida de bienes a quien fuera sorprendido leyendo una Biblia. Pero sus decretos no pudieron acortar la vida de las Escrituras ni un minuto, ni aligerar su peso ni una onza. La Biblia ha viajado por más caminos, se ha hablado en más idiomas, y ha tocado a más puertas que cualquier otro libro jamás escrito. La Escritura es santa; es completamente distinta de cualquier otro libro, porque es la Palabra viva del Dios vivo, y permanece para siempre en los cielos.

blocks.en: 6. The Word That Will Not Be Silenced
blocks.es_reference: 6. La Palabra que No Será Silenciada

blocks.en: Two Men and One Book: A man in Brazil bought a New Testament and took it home to burn. He found the fire had gone out, so he deliberately lit it again and flung the New Testament on the flames. It would not burn. He opened the pages to make it catch more easily, and it fell open to the Sermon on the Mount. He glanced at the words as the flames worked at the edges — and his mind was caught. He took the book back out, read on through the night, forgetting all time until the dawn broke, and then stood up and declared, "I believe." Another man, in Chile, found a few water-stained pages of a book washed up on the seashore after an earthquake and tidal wave. He read them and never rested until he had obtained the rest of the Bible. He not only became a Christian; he devoted the rest of his life to carrying the Scriptures into the forgotten villages of northern Chile.
blocks.es_reference: Dos Hombres y un Libro: Un hombre en Brasil compró un Nuevo Testamento y lo llevó a casa para quemarlo. Halló que el fuego se había apagado, así que deliberadamente lo encendió de nuevo y arrojó el Nuevo Testamento a las llamas. No ardía. Abrió las páginas para que prendiera más fácilmente, y se abrió en el Sermón del Monte. Echó un vistazo a las palabras mientras las llamas trabajaban los bordes — y su mente quedó cautivada. Sacó el libro, leyó toda la noche, olvidando el tiempo hasta que rompió el alba, y entonces se puso de pie y declaró: "Creo." Otro hombre, en Chile, halló unas páginas manchadas de agua de un libro arrastradas a la orilla del mar tras un terremoto y un maremoto. Las leyó y no descansó hasta obtener el resto de la Biblia. No solo llegó a ser cristiano; dedicó el resto de su vida a llevar las Escrituras a las aldeas olvidadas del norte de Chile.

blocks.en: You cannot burn this Book out of the world, and you cannot wash it away. It has a life of its own, because it is the Word of the One who lives forever.
blocks.es_reference: No se puede quemar este Libro para sacarlo del mundo, ni se le puede arrastrar con el agua. Tiene vida propia, porque es la Palabra de Aquel que vive para siempre.

blocks.en: 7. The Love of the Law
blocks.es_reference: 7. El Amor a la Ley

blocks.en: Psalm 119:97 (NKJV): "Oh, how I love Your law! It is my meditation all the day."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 119:97 (RVG): "¡Oh, cuánto amo yo tu ley! Todo el día es ella mi meditación."

blocks.en: The psalmist does not merely study the Word or obey it from duty — he loves it. It is his meditation all the day, the thing his mind returns to when it is free to go where it pleases. This is the difference between religion as a burden and religion as a delight. When you truly love someone, you want to hear their voice, you turn their words over in your mind, you keep their letters. The believer who loves God loves to hear Him speak, and God speaks in His Word. To meditate on the law all the day is simply to keep company with the God who wrote it.
blocks.es_reference: El salmista no solo estudia la Palabra ni la obedece por deber — la ama. Es su meditación todo el día, aquello a lo que su mente regresa cuando queda libre para ir a donde quiera. Esta es la diferencia entre la religión como carga y la religión como deleite. Cuando uno verdaderamente ama a alguien, quiere oír su voz, repasa sus palabras en la mente, guarda sus cartas. El creyente que ama a Dios ama oírle hablar, y Dios habla en Su Palabra. Meditar en la ley todo el día es sencillamente estar en compañía del Dios que la escribió.

blocks.en: 8. Honest Before God
blocks.es_reference: 8. Honestos Delante de Dios

blocks.en: All the psalms are designed to teach us to do one thing: to worship. They reflect every human emotion, but they do so in a distinct and important way — they are emotions seen in relationship to God. Every psalm is written in the presence of God, and so this whole book teaches us how to be honest before Him. If you have a problem, tell God about it. Do not hide it, do not cover it up, and above all do not get pious and try to smooth it over. If you are angry, say so. If you are resentful, bring it out. If you are happy, express it. That is what worship is: a heart's honesty in the presence of God. As Jesus told the woman at the well, "The true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth," and that is the kind of worshiper God is seeking.
blocks.es_reference: Todos los salmos están diseñados para enseñarnos a hacer una cosa: adorar. Reflejan toda emoción humana, pero lo hacen de una manera distinta e importante — son emociones vistas en relación con Dios. Cada salmo está escrito en la presencia de Dios, y por eso todo este libro nos enseña a ser honestos delante de Él. Si tiene un problema, dígaselo a Dios. No lo esconda, no lo encubra, y sobre todo no se ponga piadoso tratando de disimularlo. Si está enojado, dígalo. Si está resentido, sáquelo. Si está feliz, expréselo. Eso es la adoración: la honestidad del corazón en la presencia de Dios. Como Jesús dijo a la mujer junto al pozo: "Los verdaderos adoradores adorarán al Padre en espíritu y en verdad," y esa es la clase de adorador que Dios busca.

blocks.en: Think of the old story of a converted miser, long known as a stingy man. After his conversion a neighbor suffered a serious loss, and the former miser's first thought was, "They need help; I will take them a ham from my smokehouse." But on the way his old nature whispered, "Why a whole ham? Half a ham will be plenty." He debated it the whole way. Then he remembered what he had resolved in the presence of God — that by grace he would stand against the old evil whenever it asserted itself. When the tempter kept whispering, "Give him half," the old man finally said, "Look, Satan, if you don't pipe down, I'll give him the whole smokehouse." That is what grace does. Where sin abounds, grace abounds much more — and that is the purpose of the psalms: to bring us to grace, and to teach us to love the God who speaks to us in His Word.
blocks.es_reference: Piense en la vieja historia de un avaro convertido, conocido por mucho tiempo como un hombre tacaño. Después de su conversión un vecino sufrió una pérdida seria, y el primer pensamiento del antiguo avaro fue: "Necesitan ayuda; les llevaré un jamón de mi ahumadero." Pero en el camino su vieja naturaleza susurró: "¿Por qué un jamón entero? Medio jamón será suficiente." Lo debatió todo el camino. Entonces recordó lo que había resuelto en la presencia de Dios — que por gracia se opondría al viejo mal cada vez que se asomara. Cuando el tentador seguía susurrando: "Dale la mitad," el anciano al fin dijo: "Mira, Satanás, si no te callas, le daré todo el ahumadero." Eso es lo que hace la gracia. Donde el pecado abundó, sobreabundó la gracia — y ese es el propósito de los salmos: traernos a la gracia, y enseñarnos a amar al Dios que nos habla en Su Palabra.

mc.stem: What distinction does Psalm 119 hold among the chapters of the Bible?
options: It is the longest chapter in the Bible
It is the only psalm by Moses
It contains no mention of the law
mc.why: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible — 176 verses — and nearly every one exalts the Word of God.

mc.stem: How is Psalm 119 structured as a poem?
options: As a song with a repeating chorus
As a dialogue between two voices
As an acrostic in 22 sections, one for each Hebrew letter
mc.why: It is an acrostic of 22 sections, one for each Hebrew letter — a carefully crafted anthem to Scripture.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, which two psalms are devoted entirely to the Word of God?
mc.why: Two psalms are devoted wholly to the Word of God: Psalm 19 and Psalm 119.

mc.stem: The lesson describes three meanings of "the Word of God." Which set is correct?
mc.why: 'Word of God' carries three meanings: the prophetic word, the living Word (Jesus), and the written Word (the Bible).

mc.stem: What did King Solomon ask God for when offered anything he wished?
options: A great name among the nations
mc.why: Offered anything, Solomon asked for wisdom from God — still the greatest need we can bring to Him.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is the FIRST place God's wisdom comes to us, per James 1:5?
options: Through prayer — asking God, who gives liberally
mc.why: The first place wisdom comes is prayer: James 1:5 says God gives liberally to all who ask Him.

mc.stem: In the lesson, who gave Moses the wise counsel to appoint judges to share the load?
mc.why: Godly counsel is a second source of wisdom; Jethro counseled Moses to appoint judges to share the load.

mc.stem: How does the lesson say we recognize when counsel truly comes from the Lord?
options: It always agrees with our wishes
It comes only from ordained ministers
mc.why: We know counsel is from the Lord when it 'sounds like Jesus' — agreeing with His character and His Word.

mc.stem: According to Psalm 119:105, what is God's word to our feet and path?
options: A lamp to the feet and a light to the path
mc.why: Psalm 119:105 calls God's Word a lamp to the feet and a light to the path — guidance for the next step and the whole journey.

mc.stem: In the story of the ward sister in England, what finally brought her to faith?
options: A sermon she heard on the radio
Reading a copy of John's Gospel left on the ward
mc.why: The ward sister found faith by simply reading John's Gospel — the Word itself brought her to the Savior.

mc.stem: According to Psalm 119:11, why does the psalmist hide God's word in his heart?
options: That he might not sin against God
mc.why: Psalm 119:11 says the Word is hidden in the heart so that we might not sin against God — it guards from within.

mc.stem: In the story of the boy whose Bible was thrown into the fire, why was he smiling?
options: He had another Bible hidden away
He knew his father would relent
The word was hidden in his heart, which could not be burned
mc.why: The boy smiled because the Word hidden in his heart could not be burned — what is treasured within is beyond reach.

mc.stem: According to Psalm 119:89, where is God's word settled forever?
options: Written on the hearts of kings
mc.why: Psalm 119:89 declares God's Word is settled forever in heaven — fixed and unchanging beyond every earthly power.

mc.stem: What did Henry V of England do regarding the Bible, according to the lesson?
options: He had it translated into English
He passed a law threatening death or loss of property for reading a Bible
He gave a Bible to every household
He built a great library of Scriptures
mc.why: Henry V passed a law threatening death or loss of property for reading a Bible — yet the Word outlived his decree.

mc.stem: What point does the lesson make about Henry V's decrees against the Bible?
options: They could not shorten its life by a minute or lighten its weight by an ounce
They caused the Bible to be lost for centuries
mc.why: No ruler's decree could shorten the Bible's life by a minute or lighten its weight by an ounce — it cannot be destroyed.

mc.stem: The stories of the New Testament that would not burn in Brazil and the Bible pages that survived in Chile together teach what?
options: That the Word of God has a living power and outlasts every attempt to destroy it
mc.why: The Bibles that would not burn in Brazil and survived in Chile show the Word has a living power that outlasts its enemies.

mc.stem: In both the Brazil and Chile accounts, what did the men do once they had read the Scriptures?
options: They came to faith — and one gave his life to carry the Scriptures to others
They sold the pages for profit
They warned others against the Bible
mc.why: Once they read the Scriptures, the men came to faith — and one gave his life to carry the Word to others.

mc.stem: According to Psalm 119:97, what is the psalmist's relationship to God's law?
options: He fears it as a heavy burden
He loves it; it is his meditation all the day
He studies it only on the Sabbath
He has forgotten most of it
mc.why: Psalm 119:97 shows the goal: not duty but love — 'Oh, how I love Your law! It is my meditation all the day.'

mc.stem: According to the lesson, all the psalms are designed to teach us to do what one thing?
mc.why: All the psalms are finally designed to teach us one thing: to worship God honestly in His presence.

mc.stem: What does the story of the converted miser and the smokehouse illustrate about grace?
options: That the rich cannot be saved
That old habits can never change
That where sin abounds, grace abounds much more
mc.why: The converted miser and the smokehouse show that where sin abounds, grace abounds much more.

sa.prompt: Describe what makes Psalm 119 unique among the chapters of the Bible, in both its length and its structure.
sa.model: Psalm 119 is unique among the chapters of the Bible in both its length and its structure. It is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with 176 verses. And it is a carefully crafted acrostic poem of twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with every verse in a section beginning with that letter. Almost every single verse exalts the Word of God under one of its many names, law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments. It is the great sustained anthem of a believer who has fallen in love with the Scriptures.

sa.prompt: Explain the three meanings of "the Word of God" given in the lesson.
sa.model: The lesson gives three meanings of "the Word of God." First, the prophetic Word, the message God spoke through His prophets. Second, the living Word, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, who is called the Word made flesh. Third, the written Word, the Bible, the book we hold in our hands. All three are God speaking to us. Psalm 119 is chiefly about the written Word, but it teaches us to treasure all of God's speaking with the whole heart, since each one is a way the living God makes Himself known.

sa.prompt: According to the lesson, what are the three places God's wisdom comes to us? Explain each.
sa.model: The lesson names three places God's wisdom comes to us. First, through prayer: James 1:5 promises that if we lack wisdom and ask God, who gives liberally, it will be given. Second, through godly counsel, the wise words of mature believers who help us see our way, as Jethro counseled Moses. Third, and most importantly, through the written Word of God, the Bible, which is a lamp to our feet and a light to our path. Prayer, counsel, and Scripture work together, and Scripture is the surest of the three because it is God's own settled Word.

sa.prompt: What does the account of Jethro and Moses (Exodus 18) teach about seeking godly counsel as one of the places God's wisdom comes to us?
sa.model: When Moses tried to judge all the people's disputes alone, he was overwhelmed, until his father-in-law Jethro gave him wise counsel: appoint God-honoring men to share the load and judge the smaller matters. Moses listened, and the burden was shared so that many were served. The account teaches that godly counsel is one of the real ways God's wisdom reaches us. We are not meant to figure out everything alone; God often speaks through the wise, godly people He places around us, and we recognize true counsel because it agrees with His character and His Word.

sa.prompt: Explain Psalm 119:105 ("a lamp to my feet"). How does the account of the ward sister show the Word guiding a lost person to the Savior?
sa.model: Psalm 119:105 says God's Word is "a lamp to my feet and a light to my path", giving light enough for the next step and light enough for the whole journey. The world tries every other path to satisfaction and comes up empty, but the Word guides pilgrims home. The ward sister had waded through book after book and philosophy after philosophy and found life meaningless, having been argued out of trusting the Bible. When she finally read John's Gospel, she believed, saying she heard the truth and found her Savior. The lamp had been within her reach the whole time; the Word itself led her home.

sa.prompt: Explain Psalm 119:11 (hiding the word in the heart). How does the account of the boy whose Bible was burned show why this matters?
sa.model: Psalm 119:11 says, "Your word I have hidden in my heart, that I might not sin against You." The Word is not merely kept on a shelf but treasured within, where it becomes a guard against sin. The boy whose father snatched his Bible and threw it into the fire was found smiling, because, he said, "you cannot burn this in here," pointing to his heart. People may take away the printed page, but they cannot reach what is hidden in the heart. That is why memorizing and treasuring Scripture matters so deeply: what is stored within is both a defense against temptation and a possession no enemy can confiscate.

sa.prompt: Using Psalm 119:89 and the example of Henry V, explain how God's word outlasts its enemies.
sa.model: Psalm 119:89 declares, "Forever, O LORD, Your word is settled in heaven." God's Word has outlasted every ruler who tried to destroy it. Henry V of England once made Bible reading a crime, threatening death or loss of property to anyone caught reading one. Yet his decree could not shorten the life of the Scriptures by a single minute or lighten their weight by an ounce. The Bible has traveled more roads and outlived more enemies than any book ever written. Because it is the living Word of the living God, settled in heaven itself, no earthly power can ever abolish it.

sa.prompt: What do the accounts from Brazil and Chile show about the living power of the Scriptures to reach and change people?
sa.model: In Brazil a man tried twice to burn a New Testament, but it would not burn; it fell open to the Sermon on the Mount, his mind was caught, and by dawn he declared, "I believe." In Chile a man found a few water-stained Bible pages washed up after an earthquake, read them, and never rested until he had the whole Bible, then gave his life to carrying the Scriptures to forgotten villages. Both accounts show the living power of the Word: you cannot burn it out of the world or wash it away. It has a life of its own and reaches, converts, and transforms those who encounter it.

sa.prompt: Explain Psalm 119:97 and the difference between religion as a burden and religion as a delight.
sa.model: Psalm 119:97 says, "Oh, how I love Your law! It is my meditation all the day." This marks the difference between religion as a burden and religion as a delight. The psalmist does not merely study or obey the Word from duty; he loves it, and his mind returns to it freely whenever it can. When we truly love someone, we long to hear their voice and treasure their words; so the believer who loves God loves to hear Him speak in His Word. To meditate on it all the day is simply to keep glad company with the God who wrote it.

sa.prompt: According to the lesson, what is the great purpose of all the psalms, and what does it mean to be honest before God? Use the smokehouse story.
sa.model: According to the lesson, the great purpose of all the psalms is to teach us to worship, and at the heart of worship is honesty before God. The psalms reflect every human emotion, but always in relationship to God and in His presence. So they teach us to bring Him everything: if we have a problem, to tell Him; if we are angry or resentful or glad, to say so honestly rather than putting on a pious mask. The smokehouse story, where a converted miser fought his old stinginess out loud before God, shows this honesty, and shows that where sin abounds, grace abounds much more.
